catalog_quote: Stress, length and high pitch are non-phonemic. They are closely linked in that the stressed syllable usually takes high pitch. Because stress is non-phonemic, it is not of high importance and though general tendencies are evident, fluctuations are frequent with different speakers, speed of utterance and position of word in utterance. Generally, the primary stress of a word is penultimate. ... 2 syllable words: the minimum length of words in Bunama is 2 syllables with stress on the initial syllable. ... In a few examples there is fluctuation of stress on initial and final syllable. [p. 49] ... 3 syllable words: As the usual pattern, these take stress on the medial syllable, though there is also frequent occurrence of stress on the initial syllable. ... With some words, there is fluctuation of stress on initial and medial syllable. ... Words of more than 3 syllables fall into groups of 2 or 3 syllables, with the tress [sic] of the regular 2, 3 pattern. 4 syllable words: As the usual pattern, 4 syllable words group into 2 groups of 2 syllables with stress on the initial syllable of each group [p. 50] ... Where there is reduplication (a common feature of the language), and the necessity for penultimate primary stress, results in a 2+2+2 grouping [p. 54] ... the addition of the suffix /-na/ shifts the stress from its position in the 6 syllable word to the normal penultimate position [p. 54]

They are closely linked in that the stressed syllable usually takes high pitch. Because stress is non-phonemic, it is not of high importance and though general tendencies are evident, fluctuations are frequent with different speakers, speed of utterance and position of word in utterance. Generally, the primary stress of a word is penultimate.' Then '6.3.2 [handwritten: Patterns of Stress] / 6.3.2.1 Stress / 2…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-contrastive and falls, as the general rule, on the penultimate syllable of the word: initial syllable in disyllables, medial in trisyllables. Words of four or more syllables are parsed into groups of two or three syllables (following the morphology: reduplicants, roots, affixes), each group stressed on its own initial/penultimate syllable, with the word-level primary stress on the penult; adding a suffix shifts the stress rightward to keep it penultimate.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not labelled 'secondary', but longer words are described as falling into 2- and 3-syllable groups each carrying a stress (e.g. hadahada ('hada'hada) 2+2; yaloyaloha ('yaloya'loha) 3+2; to?uto?upana 2+2+2; words up to 12 syllables follow the same grouping), i.e. a rhythmic pattern of stresses every second or third syllable with the penult carrying the primary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: A few disyllables fluctuate between initial and final stress (lagim 'prow-board', ?itam 'she squeezed'); trisyllables frequently show initial instead of medial stress (deina, menena, ?enana, datule fluctuate); some 4-syllable words carry stress on the second syllable only (nuwatuhu 'thought', hepwetulu, siteluwa 'they two', ?ihapwesa 'he arrived'); derived nouns tend to keep the stress of the root (mebunama, tosamala); the minimum word is 2 syllables except the monosyllabic connectors ma, ta, be, bo and a few CVC words. Adding a suffix realigns stress so that the penult is stressed again.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (phonological word, incl. affixed and reduplicated forms); the authors note fluctuation by speaker, speed and position of the word in the utterance. §6.3.2.2 adds that within an utterance the primary stress (often with length) falls on the last of the stressed syllables, and §6.3.3 that pitch rises on the syllable of primary stress over a falling intonation contour. Corroborated first-hand by Lithgow 1992 Bunama OPD p. 3: "Stress is not phonemic. In two-syllable words the stress is on the first syllable, three syllable words take stress on the medial syllable." (file).
new_statements.identity_note: Leckie & Hughes 1976 describe the Bunama of the southern part of Normanby Island (between Sewa Bay and the eastern end; ca. 1,050 speakers at the time; main consultant Dipastine Ron), the variety Lithgow 1976 (PL C-39, pp. 445-449) separated from Duau [duau1242 area] with dialects Barabara, Bunama and Sawatupwa; Lithgow 1992 OPD places it at Sehulea, villages Gui, Barabara, Bunama, Sawatupwa. This is the language-level buna1276; no dialect-level glottocodes exist. Note the title-page author order (Leckie & Hughes) differs from Glottolog's (Hughes & Leckie).

new_statements.quote: The repetitive verb phrase signals prolongation or repetition of the action. Sometimes the vowel of the penultimate syllable of the last verb in the phrase(with clause primary stress) is notably lengthened with rapidly falling intonation on the final syllable.
new_statements.citation: Hughes, Ngaire. 1976. Bunama Phrases. Ms., SIL, Ukarumpa. 39 pp. SIL archives entry 56364.
new_statements.locator: §I.4 Repetitive Verb Phrase, p. 6 (handwritten page number; p. 7)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (the PDF's metadata: 40 pp, image-only) and the page imagehandwritten page number 6, header 'Bunama', section 'I.4. Repetitive Verb Phrase'). The quoted passage is on that page word for word: 'The repetitive verb phrase signals prolongation or repetition of the action. Sometimes the vowel of the penultimate syllable of the last verb in the phrase(with clause primary stress) is notably lengthened with rapidly falling intonation on the final syllable.' (no space before the parenthesis, 'syllable' has a typewriter overstrike but reads syllable). The examples that follow ('i-hane-ma 'i-hane-ma 'i-haneeee-ma; si-hiyahiya x5; ta-miya-lugu-wa x3) show the lengthening but carry no stress mar…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's penultimate placement; adds only a phrase-level detail (clause primary stress on the last verb of a repetitive verb phrase, penultimate vowel lengthening, falling final intonation). No new word-level rule. The rest of the 39 pages (verbal and non-verbal phrase types, possession, coordination, relator-axis phrases) says nothing about stress, accent, tone or pitch (checked by a full-text search for stress/accent/prominence/tone/pitch/intonation/length and fuzzy scanned variants).
new_statements.rule_in_words: This is a phrase-level syntax ms with no phonology section; the only prosodic remark is that in repetitive verb phrases the phrase-final verb carries the clause's primary stress and its penultimate vowel is often lengthened, with a rapidly falling intonation on the final syllable. It gives no explicit word-stress rule, but the lengthened, prominent syllable is the penultimate one, consistent with the penultimate word stress described in Leckie & Hughes 1976 (where stress, length and high pitch co-occur).
new_statements.exceptions: None; the lengthening is described as occasional ('Sometimes').
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe Bunama proper (Lithgow 1987 p. 1: 'The Bunama language area is the south-eastern part of Normanby Island'); Lithgow 1987/1989 is primarily about Dobu with Bunama and Bwaidoka comparison. No sub-dialect is named in either.
